intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that stomatin-deficient cryohydrocytosis with neurologic defects (SDCHCN) is caused by mutation in the SLC2A1 gene, which encodes the glucose transporter GLUT1.

paragraphs.text: Stomatin-deficient cryohydrocytosis (sdCHC) is a rare form of hereditary stomatocytosis in which the red cell membrane leaks sodium and potassium, and the leak becomes much worse in the cold. Patients have hemolytic anemia and hepatosplenomegaly. They also have neurologic and other defects, including cataracts, seizures, mental retardation, and movement disorder (Fricke et al., 2004; Flatt et al., 2011). Flatt et al. (2011) regarded the disorder as a novel form of GLUT1 deficiency syndrome.

checks.evidence_quote: This report concerns congenitally Na(+)-K(+) leaky red cells of the 'hereditary stomatocytosis' class.
checks.explanation: The paper places stomatin-deficient cases in the hereditary stomatocytosis class. It also says only two cases of the cryohydrocytosis variant are known, which supports calling it rare.

paragraphs.text: Fricke et al. (2004) described 3 new isolated cases and 1 new pedigree with stomatin-deficient hereditary stomatocytosis, and expanded the description of 1 previously reported case. In all of these patients, red cells leaked cations markedly at 37 degrees C and had markedly abnormal intracellular Na and K concentrations. The cases differed in how the passive K leak depended on temperature. In 3, the leak showed a simple monotonic temperature dependence. In the other 2, the leak was lowest at about 20 to 25 degrees C, so that the cells were extremely leaky at 0 degrees C, which is the cryohydrocytosis phenotype. Fricke et al. (2004) stated that these 2 patients were the only known cases of stomatin-deficient cryohydrocytosis. Both patients had a congenital syndrome of mental retardation, seizures, cataracts, and massive hepatosplenomegaly. The authors suggested that this probably defined a new hematoneurologic syndrome.

paragraphs.text: Bawazir et al. (2012) reported an infant who presented with erratic hyperkalemia, neonatal hyperbilirubinemia, anemia, hepatic dysfunction, and microcephaly. The infant later developed seizures and had delayed developmental milestones. MRI and CT scans of the brain showed multiple abnormalities, including periventricular calcification. Vision was impaired by both cataracts and retinal dysfunction. The red cells were extremely leaky, which caused the hemolysis. Their loss of potassium depended on temperature, which explained the hyperkalemia as pseudohyperkalemia. The authors described this as the fourth pedigree reported with the syndrome.

paragraphs.text: Lande et al. (1982) studied red cell membrane proteins from 2 patients, one with hereditary stomatocytosis and one with cryohydrocytosis. On 1-dimensional SDS gel electrophoresis, the band 7 proteins separated into 3 components of approximately 30,000, 28,000, and 26,000 daltons, and the 28,000-dalton component was decreased in both patients. Two-dimensional electrophoresis split this component into 2 proteins, designated 22 x 8 and 60 x 8. In both patients, 22 x 8 was completely absent, whereas 60 x 8 was present as usual. All band 7 proteins were present in normal subjects and in reticulocytosis controls. The authors raised the possibility that loss of this protein was responsible for the increased Na and K permeability.

agent.process_note: I read all 4 papers in full; only the abstracts were available. The abstracts do not give the zygosity of the SLC2A1 mutations or how they were inherited, so I left zygosity out of the intro and recorded inheritance as UNKNOWN. Flatt et al. (2011) say hereditary stomatocytoses in general are dominantly inherited, but they do not say this of sdCHC. The Flatt et al. (2011) abstract does not name its 2 SLC2A1 mutations, so neither has an allelic-variant entry. For the Bawazir et al.
